trials.title: Give Each Dragon Its Own Name (__init__ & self)
trials.storyPrompt: To give each dragon its OWN custom name when you create it, Python uses a special setup method called `__init__`. Right now creating `Dragon("Comet")` crashes with a `TypeError`.
trials.objective: Fix the broken `Dragon` class so creating `Dragon("Comet")` stores its name and prints `Comet`.

hints.tier3_walkthrough: Change `def __init__(name):` to `def __init__(self, name):` so Python can pass the new object as `self`.

introChoice.title: Why Every Method Needs self
introChoice.prompt: To give each object its OWN data, Python runs a special setup method called `__init__` whenever you create one. So `Dragon("Comet")` below builds a new dragon and runs `__init__` to set it up. `__init__`'s FIRST parameter is ALWAYS `self` — 'this brand-new object being built right now' — so `self.name = name` can attach the name onto it.
introChoice.question: Which `__init__` line lets Python hand the new dragon in as `self`?

choices.label: Option A
choices.explanation: This is the bug waiting for you in Step 2! Python always passes the new object first, so with only one parameter there is no room for the name and `Dragon("Comet")` stops with a TypeError.

choices.label: Option B
choices.explanation: Spot on! `self` comes FIRST, then `name`. Python hands the new dragon over as `self` automatically, so `self.name = name` attaches `"Comet"` onto it.

choices.label: Option C
choices.explanation: Close, but this one accepts no name at all! `Dragon("Comet")` needs a second parameter to catch `"Comet"`.

choices.label: Option D
choices.explanation: The order matters! Python always hands over the new object FIRST, so `self` has to be the first parameter.
